slides.title: Knowles’ Andragogy Meets Critical Equity (1/2) — Malcolm Knowles (Classical Theory)
text: Knowles’ Andragogy Meets Critical Equity (1/2)
Malcolm Knowles (Classical Theory)
Self-Directed: Adults resist imposed knowledge.

Self-direction and learner autonomy quotes: “Would like more time to talk and share experience.” · “Open forum to share struggles in the role.” · “Talked about what we need, relevant, current.” (Key message: There was a clear preference for greater participant-led discussion, peer sharing and opportunities for staff to shape CPD around identified needs.)
Life Experience: Learners bring a rich reservoir of prior knowledge.

Life experience and prior knowledge quotes: “Nothing new.” · “Take into account prior knowledge.” · “We are doing things quite well already.” · “Some elements did not offer additional learning as I already do these.” (Key message: CPD did not always sufficiently recognise, build upon or extend participants’ existing knowledge and professional expertise.)
Immediate Relevance: Content must apply to current goals.

Immediate relevance and practical application quotes: “I would like to have more examples… Maybe using real-life case studies.” · “Not hugely engaging… would be better as a half-day CPD with more practical elements.” · “Slot into a different time or format. Too much student-focused work to do.” (Key message: Staff wanted more practical activity, authentic examples and case studies, with content more closely connected to immediate workplace challenges.)
Reference: Knowles, M. S. (1980). The Modern Practice of Adult Education: From Pedagogy to Andragogy. · Knowles, M. S., Holton, E. F., & Swanson, R. A. (2020). The Adult Learner (9th ed.).
slides.speakerNotes:
Knowles’ classical theory of andragogy centres on three pillars—and our own staff CPD feedback illustrates each one:
1. Self-Direction & Learner Autonomy: “Would like more time to talk and share experience.” / “Open forum to share struggles in the role.” / “Talked about what we need, relevant, current.” — Key message: There was a clear preference for greater participant-led discussion, peer sharing and opportunities for staff to shape CPD around identified needs.
2. Life Experience & Prior Knowledge: “Nothing new.” / “Take into account prior knowledge.” / “We are doing things quite well already.” / “Some elements did not offer additional learning as I already do these.” — Key message: CPD did not always sufficiently recognise, build upon or extend participants’ existing knowledge and professional expertise.
3. Immediate Relevance & Practical Application: “I would like to have more examples… Maybe using real-life case studies.” / “Not hugely engaging… would be better as a half-day CPD with more practical elements.” — Key message: Staff wanted more practical activity, authentic examples and case studies, with content more closely connected to immediate workplace challenges.
Reference: Knowles, M. S. (1980). The Modern Practice of Adult Education: From Pedagogy to Andragogy. · Knowles, M. S., Holton, E. F., & Swanson, R. A. (2020). The Adult Learner (9th ed.).

slides.title: Knowles’ Andragogy Meets Critical Equity (2/2) — The Equity Expansion (Modern Reality)
text: Knowles’ Andragogy Meets Critical Equity (2/2)
The Equity Expansion (Modern Reality)
Power Dynamics: Marginalization dictates who feels safe sharing.
Psychological Safety: Trauma and socioeconomic status condition participation.
Proactive Design: Inclusion removes barriers before adjustments are requested.
References: Brookfield, S. D. (2005). The Power of Critical Theory for Adult Learning and Teaching. · Edmondson, A. (1999). · CAST (2018). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines.
slides.speakerNotes: Knowles assumed an unencumbered, autonomous adult. In modern reality, power dynamics dictate who feels safe sharing (Brookfield, 2005), trauma and socioeconomic precarity condition participation and psychological safety (Edmondson, 1999), and proactive inclusive design must remove barriers before adjustments are requested (CAST, 2018).

text: Interactive CPD Check: Knowles’ Andragogy × Critical Equity
Quick Check: Classical Andragogy or Critical Equity Expansion?

Mode 1 — Lens Classifier (6 Scenarios): Classify real-world adult teaching and CPD scenarios between Malcolm Knowles (Classical Theory: Self-Direction, Life Experience, Immediate Relevance) and The Equity Expansion (Modern Reality: Power Dynamics, Psychological Safety, Proactive Design).
Mode 2 — Diagnostic Quiz (3 Scenarios): Diagnose why classical adult learning assumptions falter without a critical equity lens and select the inclusive redesign.
References: Knowles (1980) · Knowles, Holton & Swanson (2020) · Brookfield (2005) · Edmondson (1999) · CAST (2018).
slides.speakerNotes: Run this 2-minute interactive check with CPD attendees. In Mode 1 (Lens Classifier), invite tables or the whole room to classify each of the 6 teaching scenarios into either Malcolm Knowles' Classical Andragogy or The Equity Expansion, then click 'Check Answers' to unpack the academic rationale. Optionally switch to Mode 2 (Diagnostic Quiz) to test applied redesign decisions.

slides.title: Differentiated Pathways to Practice
text: Differentiated Pathways to Practice

Developing Practitioners — Focus: Concrete, low-prep inclusive teaching strategies. Action: Embed 2–3 ready-to-use techniques into next week's plan. Goal: Build confidence in proactive universal design.

Experienced Lecturers — Focus: Complex edge-cases balancing inclusion and professional standards. Action: Design a micro-evaluation to measure a novel adaptation's impact. Goal: Share evidence of curricular adaptation success.
slides.speakerNotes: Highlight that experienced teachers need space to wrestle with complex edge cases, while newer colleagues benefit from immediate, high-leverage procedural templates.

slides.title: Applied Case Studies: Lived Experience
text: Applied Case Studies: Lived Experience
Case Study A — Clinical Audiology: Clinical training with mature healthcare learners. Tension point: Highly demanding learners attempting to monopolise teacher support.
Case Study B — HyFlex Health: Allied health learners balancing shifts and childcare. Tension point: Extreme workloads and synchronous distance isolation.
Case Study C — Technical Education (Carpentry): Adult trade & carpentry learners retraining while working. Tension point: Strong practical know-how vs. technical vocabulary and written theory.
Listen to the case studies and think about which example best relates to your learners' challenges.

Adult learners rarely fail in isolation.
Their success is shaped by the environments we create.

slides.title: Case Study B (4/6): Three Lessons for Inclusive Adult Learning
text: Three Lessons for Inclusive Adult Learning
1. Belonging enables participation
2. Clarity reduces hidden barriers
3. Support strengthens rigour
Engagement is shaped by the learning environment.
slides.speakerNotes: Discuss belonging, clarity and support. Emphasise these are conditions that enable participation and success. From interview, establish a connection, ask questions beyond the standard (are there children at home, who is able to support you at work and at home, are you prepared for what is about to happen?). Be clear on expectations in the learning environment, particularly online (noise), formal/informal support, anxieties, community of learning ('sharing is caring, safe space and room to grow'), and academic rules and regulations.

text: Case Study C: Technical Education — Carpentry (2/2)

Multiple Means of Action: Introduce oral workshop walk-throughs and voice-note explanations.
Tech Integration: Seamless assistive technology, speech-to-text, and annotated rig diagrams.
Scaffolding: Bridge everyday workshop vernacular to technical terms via Semantic Waves.
Pedagogical Payoff: Evaluates true technical and vocational mastery without academic literacy gating.

slides.title: Semantic Waves (LCT): Tacit-to-Explicit Bridging (2/2) — Legitimation Code Theory (Maton, 2013)
text: Semantic Waves (LCT): Tacit-to-Explicit Bridging (2/2)
The Research: Legitimation Code Theory (Maton, 2013)
How knowledge moves between practical mastery and abstract theory
Practical Know-How (High Semantic Gravity · Low Semantic Density): Context-dependent, concrete workshop skill and everyday trade vernacular.
Technical Terminology (Low Semantic Gravity · High Semantic Density): Abstract concepts, condensed industry terminology, and written theory.

The 'Semantic Flatline' Trap: Adult vocational learners often get stuck in a flatline—either performing the practical skill brilliantly without passing written assessments, or memorizing abstract textbook definitions they cannot apply on the workshop floor.
Reference: Maton, K. (2013). Making semantic waves: A key to cumulative knowledge-building. Linguistics and Education, 24(1), 8–22.
slides.speakerNotes: Semantic Waves (Part 2/2): Unpack Karl Maton's (2013) Legitimation Code Theory (LCT)—contrasting Practical Know-How (high semantic gravity, low semantic density) with Technical Terminology (low semantic gravity, high semantic density)—and show how adult vocational learners get caught in a 'semantic flatline' unless teaching explicitly waves between workshop action and written theory.

slides.title: Semantic Waves: Bridging Practical & Technical
text: SCENARIO EXTENSION • SAM, 42 (MATON, 2013)
Semantic Waves: Bridging Practical & Technical
Reverse-Wave Oral-to-Written Strategy: Employ during practical observation before providing vocabulary glossaries or sentence starters.

ABSTRACT & TECHNICAL (Low Semantic Gravity) — Avoid 'semantic flatlines' by riding the wave from workshop floor to written theory — CONCRETE & PRACTICAL (High Semantic Gravity) — Legitimation Code Theory (LCT)
1. Down-Escalate (Check): Observe practical task explained in everyday workshop slang.
2. Pivot (Decide): Swap two colloquial actions for industry terms via voice-note.
3. Up-Escalate (Act): Probe system changes verbally before requiring written prose.
Diagnostic Purpose: Use before glossaries or sentence starters to separate literacy barriers from conceptual misconceptions. CHECK → DECIDE → ACT

slides.title: The Inclusion Marketplace: 5 Adult Learning Barriers
text: The Inclusion Marketplace
Time Poverty & Role Conflict: Shift work and unpredictable hours; Active parenting and intensive elder care.
Neurodivergence: High executive load for organizational tasks; Hidden exhaustion from autistic/ADHD masking.
Linguistic Diversity: The trap of hidden academic language codes; Exclusion via culturally specific examples.
Digital Divide: Reliance on mobile-only or shared devices; Low bandwidth impacting synchronous learning.
Schooling Scars: Past educational trauma in formal schooling; Persistent fear of academic exposure.
slides.speakerNotes: Frame these five barrier areas not as student deficits, but as structural interfaces. Every barrier represents an institutional design challenge that thoughtful pedagogy and Universal Design can solve.

slides.title: How the Knowledge Marketplace Works
text: How the Knowledge Marketplace Works

Step 1: Questions & Resources — Start with the 5 Barriers: Question Sheet: Each team and individual starts with questions covering all 5 barrier areas. Resource Pack: Teams receive resources describing their assigned barrier challenge and explaining solutions.

Step 2: Flipchart Poster — Build Your Marketplace Stall: Synthesise: Unpack the challenge and practical inclusive solutions from your team's resource pack. Create Poster: Produce a clear visual poster on flipchart paper to teach visiting peers.

Step 3: Explain & Explore — Host & Roam the Stalls: 1 Stays Behind: One team member remains at the flipchart poster to explain the challenge and solutions. Roam & Find Answers: Team members visit the other areas to find answers to the 5-barrier questions.
Goal: Return to your home team and share the answers gathered from all 5 barrier stations.
slides.speakerNotes: Walk participants through the three-step Knowledge Marketplace protocol: (1) review the 5-barrier question sheet and team resource pack, (2) create a flipchart poster explaining the challenge and its solutions, and (3) leave one stallholder behind to teach visitors while team researchers visit the other stations to gather answers.
